Welcome to my portfolio for MUSA 5080: Public Policy Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania.
This site documents my work in the Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program — weekly notes, course assignments, and a final project applying data analysis to urban policy questions.



I’m a student in the MUSA program at Penn. My background is in urban planning and real estate development, and I’m interested in housing, economic development, and how data and civic technology can help us better understand and build cities.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Reflection

What I want most from this course: To become comfortable enough with these tools that I can use them beyond the classroom, especially for real estate, housing, and urban research. I want to get to a point where working with data and building something from it feels natural rather than intimidating.
One thing I’m nervous about: I’m still nervous about coding and keeping track of how all the different tools connect, especially Git, GitHub, RStudio, and Quarto. But getting everything running this week made the whole process feel a little less abstract.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median household income across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NY"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B19013_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B19013_001    83149  1788
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B19013_001    61233  2429
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B19013_001    49036   872
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B19013_001    61059  1769
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B19013_001    58248  1978
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B19013_001    66583  2266


[How many rows did you get? Does that match the number of counties in your state?] I was able to find 62 rows and it matches to the number of counties in the state of New York.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York      68950  7533   10.9 
 2 Schuyler County, New York      65625  5286    8.05
 3 Yates County, New York         67521  4456    6.60
 4 Seneca County, New York        66007  3860    5.85
 5 Essex County, New York         70215  3895    5.55
 6 Montgomery County, New York    62923  3436    5.46
 7 Warren County, New York        78239  4231    5.41
 8 Orleans County, New York       63838  3328    5.21
 9 Lewis County, New York         68329  3456    5.06
10 Genesee County, New York       72055  3586    4.98


[Which county has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate? How large is it?] Hamilton County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate and its 10.925308. —

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    53
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            8


[How many counties fall into each category?] There are 53 counties counties in high confidence, 1 county in low confidence and 8 counties in moderate. —

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       83149   1788  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York     61233   2429   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York        49036    872 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       61059   1769  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York  58248   1978   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York       66583   2266   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         53        369308.
2 Moderate                 9         33224.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?] The average population for for high-confidence counties is 369307.62 versus the moderate which is 33223.89. Yes, there is pattern - counties with larger population have high confidence while counties with lower population have low-confidence. —
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.] We know the least about Hamilton County, Schuyler County and Yates County out of the 62 counties in the state of New York. And this is due to due to their smaller population number. Things could go wrong in many subsidy allocation when building public infrastructure such as road, electricity and housing. And that could affect how people live, play and work and most of all; their access to opportunities could be dramatically limited. —
